scenes.tts: How can the same offspring genotypes make groups that look different? Watch pink snapdragons send their allele copies into an empty grid. The copies will stay fixed while the phenotype rule changes around them. The screen will track inherited copies separately from the visible traits they help produce.

scenes.visual: Hook before any title: two large schematic pink snapdragons fill the frame. Each opens to reveal separate R and W tiles. Red R stays #E85D5D; pale W stays #F4E7C5. The tiles drift toward a large empty Punnett grid. Keep a small 'schematic' label visible.

scenes.visual: The carried plants and tiles shrink slightly but remain visible. Write the title 'One Cross, Three Patterns' above the grid, hold briefly, then transform the title into a small header. Tiles continue a gentle orbit.

scenes.tts: An allele is a version of a gene. Each parent can pass its red allele or its white allele. The grid tracks every pairing. It does not decide what each pairing looks like. Keeping those jobs separate is the key to reading the result.
scenes.caption: An allele is a version of a gene. Each parent can pass its R allele or its W allele. The grid tracks every pairing. It does not decide what each pairing looks like. Keeping those jobs separate is the key to reading the result.
scenes.visual: Carry the same grid. One parent's R and W tiles move across the column headers; the other's move down the row headers. Add the label 'allele pairings' beneath the grid. Leave all four cells empty and moving with faint landing targets.
scenes.narration: An allele is a version of a gene. Each parent can pass its R allele or its W allele. The grid tracks every pairing. It does not decide what each pairing looks like. Keeping those jobs separate is the key to reading the result.

scenes.tts: Before the tiles land, predict the combinations. Which pairing repeats, and which pairings appear at the corners? Hold your answer while the tiles keep moving. Look for repeated paths rather than guessing from the parents' pink color.
scenes.caption: Before the tiles land, predict the combinations. Which pairing repeats, and which pairings appear at the corners? Hold your answer while the tiles keep moving. Look for repeated paths rather than guessing from the parents' pink color.
scenes.visual: Replace the header with the question. Four R or W tiles glide slowly around the empty cells without landing. Highlight the two diagonal landing paths in turn, but reveal no genotype.
scenes.narration: Before the tiles land, predict the combinations. Which pairing repeats, and which pairings appear at the corners? Hold your answer while the tiles keep moving. Look for repeated paths rather than guessing from the parents' pink color.

scenes.visual: Keep the prediction question and empty grid on screen. The allele tiles continue slow motion around their landing targets. A thin thinking ring completes one calm loop; show no answer.

scenes.tts: The tiles land as red-red, red-white, red-white, and white-white. The mixed pairing appears twice. This genotype pattern comes from allele separation, so changing the phenotype rule cannot change the grid. The parents' pink phenotype never fused their red and white allele copies.
scenes.caption: The tiles land as RR, RW, RW, and WW. The mixed pairing appears twice. This genotype pattern comes from allele separation, so changing the phenotype rule cannot change the grid. The parents' pink phenotype never fused their R and W allele copies.
scenes.visual: Land the four tile pairs in order, then pulse the two RW cells together. Build an on-screen genotype bar from the computed grid: RR | RW RW | WW, with 'genotypes stay fixed' beneath it.
scenes.narration: The tiles land as RR, RW, RW, and WW. The mixed pairing appears twice. This genotype pattern comes from allele separation, so changing the phenotype rule cannot change the grid. The parents' pink phenotype never fused their R and W allele copies.

scenes.tts: Now place an incomplete-dominance lens over the grid. Red-red becomes red, white-white becomes white, and red-white becomes pink. Every genotype has its own phenotype here, so the phenotype pattern matches the genotype pattern. The color looks blended, but the inherited copies remain distinct inside each plant.
scenes.caption: Now place an incomplete-dominance lens over the grid. RR becomes red, WW becomes white, and RW becomes pink. Every genotype has its own phenotype here, so the phenotype pattern matches the genotype pattern. The color looks blended, but the inherited copies remain distinct inside each plant.
scenes.visual: Slide a large labelled lens 'incomplete dominance' over the unchanged tiles. Beneath each cell, grow a schematic flower: red, pink, pink, white. Transform the genotype bar into a phenotype bar while keeping the tile pairs visible above it.
scenes.narration: Now place an incomplete-dominance lens over the grid. RR becomes red, WW becomes white, and RW becomes pink. Every genotype has its own phenotype here, so the phenotype pattern matches the genotype pattern. The color looks blended, but the inherited copies remain distinct inside each plant.

scenes.tts: Codominance needs a different gene, so switch to Shorthorn cattle. The same three pairings give red, roan and white coats. A roan red-white calf grows red hairs and white hairs side by side. The mixed genotype shows both effects instead of an in-between color. The allele pairings still do not move.
scenes.caption: Codominance needs a different gene, so switch to Shorthorn cattle. The same three pairings give red, roan and white coats. A roan RW calf grows red hairs and white hairs side by side. The mixed genotype shows both effects instead of an in-between color. The allele pairings still do not move.
scenes.visual: Relabel the grid 'Shorthorn coat color' and change the lens label to 'codominance'. Keep the R and W tiles and all four pairings unchanged. Replace the flowers under all four cells with large schematic coat patches: RR solid red, both RW cells alternating red and pale hairs, WW pale. Never blend the R and W tile colors.
scenes.narration: Codominance needs a different gene, so switch to Shorthorn cattle. The same three pairings give red, roan and white coats. A roan RW calf grows red hairs and white hairs side by side. The mixed genotype shows both effects instead of an in-between color. The allele pairings still do not move.

scenes.tts: Alleles remain separate, and each genetic tool reveals a different scale. The grid reveals allele combinations. A phenotype key reveals how each combination appears. Confusing those views makes pink look like permanent blending. The tool must match the question you are asking.

scenes.visual: Split the carried world into aligned layers without cutting away: allele tiles on top, computed grid in the middle, schematic phenotype strip below. A vertical bracket labels the layers 'alleles', 'genotypes', and 'phenotypes'.
scenes.narration: Alleles remain separate, and each genetic tool reveals a different scale. The grid reveals allele combinations. A phenotype key reveals how each combination appears. Confusing those views makes pink look like permanent blending. The tool must match the question you are asking.

scenes.tts: The same separation helps with blood type. A population has three common ABO alleles, but each person carries a pair. Type AB red blood cells display both A and B markers, a codominant phenotype. Type O cells display neither marker, while type A or B displays its matching marker.
scenes.caption: The same separation helps with blood type. A population has three common ABO alleles, but each person carries a pair. Type AB red blood cells display both A and B markers, a codominant phenotype. Type O cells display neither marker, while type A or B displays its matching marker.
scenes.visual: Slide the genotype grid left but keep it visible. On the right, build one large schematic red blood cell. Place labelled A marker blocks in red and B marker blocks in blue on its edge. Label 'type AB: both marker types'. No molecular structures.
scenes.narration: The same separation helps with blood type. A population has three common ABO alleles, but each person carries a pair. Type AB red blood cells display both A and B markers, a codominant phenotype. Type O cells display neither marker, while type A or B displays its matching marker.

scenes.tts: So do not ask which allele won. Ask which alleles were inherited, then ask what that pair does to phenotype. The first answer comes from the cross. The second comes from the inheritance pattern. That order keeps inheritance separate from the way a trait is displayed.
